opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think priors matter a lot here, and people often underrate how much of their view is coming from the prior rather than from the evidence.

One way I think about it: if you'd asked me a decade ago, before scaling had really taken off, you'd have a fairly diffuse prior over when we get AI that can do roughly everything a human expert can do. You might spread your probability over many decades, maybe with a long tail out to "this takes a century or more." Then you look at the evidence of the last several years: models getting dramatically better at coding, math, and agentic tasks, the length of tasks they can complete autonomously growing pretty steadily, and compute going up by large factors each year. That evidence pushes you toward shorter timelines. But how far it pushes you depends a lot on where you started.

There are a couple of priors I find myself weighing. One is a sort of outside-view prior that says transformative technologies usually take a long time, things are always harder than they look, and the last 10% takes 90% of the effort. That pushes toward longer timelines and toward discounting impressive benchmarks. The other is more like: we're scaling inputs, compute and algorithmic progress, at an extraordinary rate, and that rate can't continue forever. Either we hit something like full automation of AI R&D in the next several years while scaling continues, or progress slows a lot once we hit the limits on how fast we can grow compute and spending. That gives you a distribution that's front-loaded: a substantial chunk of probability in the next five-ish years, then a long, flatter tail after that.

I personally put a lot of weight on that second framing. So I end up with something like: a meaningful probability, maybe on the order of a quarter, that we get AIs capable of automating most AI research within roughly the next few years, and if it doesn't happen by around the end of the decade, my yearly probability drops quite a bit. That's not because I think it becomes impossible. It's because the main driver, rapid input scaling, would be running out of steam.

The other thing I'd flag is that people with very short timelines and people with very long timelines often look at the same evidence and update in opposite directions, partly because of their priors about what the remaining gaps are. If you think the missing pieces are a few qualitative capabilities, like long-horizon agency, reliability, or sample-efficient learning, you might think they'll fall to scale the way earlier gaps did. If you think they're deep and require fundamentally new ideas, you'll be much more skeptical. I'm genuinely uncertain there, and I think the honest position is wide error bars with a lot of mass relatively soon. Concretely, that means we should be preparing for the short-timelines worlds, because those are the worlds where safety work is most urgent and we have the least slack.

r001.rationale: The response says recent progress and scaling put substantial probability on AI research automation soon, but does not cite the relatively short time spent on AI research as a reason this outcome is not unlikely on prior grounds.

r002.rationale: It describes an outside-view prior that pushes toward longer timelines, but says Greenblatt personally puts more weight on the shorter-timeline framing. It does not state that prior-based expectations pull him toward longer timelines overall.

r003.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about whether remaining capabilities will emerge through scaling or require fundamentally new ideas, and says it is genuinely uncertain about those gaps.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think priors matter a lot here, and I want to be careful about which priors we're talking about, because people often mean different things.

One version is something like: historically, big technological transitions take a long time, and people who predict that some transformative technology is right around the corner have usually been wrong. That's a real consideration, and I do think it should pull you toward longer timelines than you'd get if you just extrapolated the last three years of progress naively. If you'd been looking at AI in, say, 1970 or 1985, and you'd been very excited, you'd have been burned. So some skepticism is warranted.

But I think the way I actually try to use priors is a bit different. I start from something like: how much do I expect the current paradigm to continue delivering if we keep scaling up compute, data, and the amount of effort going into algorithmic improvements? And then I ask what the trend looks like. And when I look at things like the length of tasks that models can complete autonomously, that's been doubling on a pretty fast cadence, something on the order of every several months. If you just extrapolate that, you get to systems that can do very long, very hard tasks pretty soon, like within a few years. So the inside-view trend extrapolation gives you fairly short timelines.

Then the prior comes in as a check on that. I ask myself, how often do trends like this just keep going versus hitting some wall? And my honest answer is that trends do often continue longer than people expect, but they also sometimes bend. Compute scaling in particular is going to run into real constraints, with power, with chip production, with how much money people are willing to spend, probably within this decade. So I put real probability mass on the trend slowing down for reasons that have nothing to do with the underlying capabilities not being achievable.

The net effect is that I end up with something like a 25 percent chance of very powerful AI, the kind that could automate most of AI research, by around 2029, with maybe a 50 percent chance by the early-to-mid 2030s. And a lot of the remaining mass is spread out over a fairly long tail where things turn out harder than they look. I don't think the priors push me to say it's basically impossible soon. I think they push me away from saying it's overwhelmingly likely soon.

One thing I'd add is that I think people sometimes over-apply the reference class of "past predictions of AI were wrong." The people who were wrong in the past didn't have a trend of rapidly improving general-purpose systems to point to. They had hopes about a method. Now we have a method that is in fact working, and the question is more about how far it goes and how fast, rather than whether it works at all. That's a different epistemic situation, and I think the prior should be updated to reflect that, even if it shouldn't be thrown out.

r001.rationale: The response discusses past AI predictions and says current methods are working, but it does not identify the relatively short time spent on AI research as a reason powerful AI soon is not unlikely on prior grounds.

r002.rationale: It says historical priors should pull timelines longer than recent-trend extrapolation would suggest and reduce confidence that powerful AI is overwhelmingly likely soon.

r003.rationale: The response allows that trends may bend and that progress may prove harder, but it does not question how confidently the next stage of AI progress is achievable; it says the current method is working and frames the uncertainty mainly around how far and how fast it goes.

astra-6.text:
I think priors matter quite a bit, because the evidence we have doesn’t uniquely determine a timeline. You can look at the same progress and come away with different expectations depending on how hard you thought the remaining problems were going to be.

For example, if you start with a strong expectation that human intelligence involves lots of distinct insights that we haven’t discovered yet, then recent progress might look like we’ve solved one part of the problem. If you think intelligence is more a matter of learning sufficiently general patterns with enough computation, that same progress looks much more suggestive that we’re getting close.

My inclination is to put substantial weight on the empirical evidence: what systems can do, how that changes with scale, and whether apparent bottlenecks persist. But there’s still a prior involved in extrapolating those trends. We haven’t observed the transition to systems that can automate essentially all intellectual work, so we can’t just read the answer off a graph.

So I’d want to be suspicious of both a very confident long timeline based on the idea that intelligence must be profoundly difficult, and a very confident short timeline based on a smooth extrapolation. I think relatively short timelines are a serious possibility, but there’s substantial uncertainty about how much further the current approaches will take us and how quickly the remaining gaps can be closed.

r001.rationale: The response says the evidence and priors leave timelines uncertain, but it does not cite AI research having been brief as a reason powerful AI could arrive soon.

r002.rationale: It describes priors that could support longer timelines, but does not say prior-based expectations pull Ryan toward longer timelines.

r003.rationale: It notes that the transition to systems able to automate essentially all intellectual work has not been observed and questions how far current approaches will take us or how quickly remaining gaps can be closed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think priors matter quite a bit, especially when we’re trying to extrapolate beyond the systems we can actually observe. But I don’t think there’s some uniquely correct prior that tells us when powerful AI is going to arrive.

For example, you might start with the intuition that automating essentially all cognitive work would be an extraordinary historical event, so it probably isn’t happening in the next few years. That’s a reasonable starting point. But you need to update that view based on what AI systems can already do, how quickly those capabilities have improved, and how much further we can scale the approaches that are working.

My inclination is to put more weight on that concrete evidence than on a broad prior that transformative changes are rare. At the same time, there are substantial uncertainties about whether current approaches will encounter obstacles, and how hard those obstacles will be to overcome. So I end up with a fairly broad distribution over arrival times, including substantial probability on powerful AI arriving quite soon.

r001.rationale: The response gives the prior that automating cognitive work would be an extraordinary event, but does not mention how little time AI research has had or use that as a reason a soon arrival is plausible.

r002.rationale: It says concrete evidence matters more than a broad prior that transformative changes are rare, and does not say priors pull Greenblatt toward longer timelines.

r003.rationale: It explicitly raises uncertainty about whether current approaches will encounter obstacles and how hard those obstacles will be to overcome, questioning confidence in further progress.
